title: Set up your environment
description: Run a first MicroPython program in the micro:bit simulator, use serial/REPL and sensor controls, and run the lab tests locally.
outcome: You can run any lab in the browser simulator, read its serial output, poke it from the REPL, and run its logic tests on your PC.
environment: micro:bit Python Editor v3 (python.microbit.org) with its MicroPython micro:bit V2 simulator (iframe python-simulator.usermbit.org/v/0.1; MIT; embeds MicroPython for micro:bit 2.1.1 per the repo's lib folder). Local: Python 3.12 stdlib + labs/sim_stub. CI: Node 24 + @playwright/test 1.64.1. Hosts: Apple-silicon Mac mini (macOS 14+) and Windows 11, same browser simulator; tests run with python3 (macOS) / py (Windows); see documentation/HARDWARE.md.
overview: The micro:bit Python Editor includes a simulated micro:bit V2 that runs real MicroPython (compiled to WebAssembly), so no board is needed.
Each lab's logic is also unit-tested on your PC against a small stub of the microbit module.
prerequisites: A current desktop browser with internet access (the editor must load online)

glossary.meaning: Software micro:bit V2 in the browser; runs MicroPython and offers sliders/buttons for sensors.
Text channel from the program (print) to the computer; shown in the editor's serial panel.
Read-Evaluate-Print-Loop: type Python lines and see results immediately.
Fake module with the same API as the real one, used only for tests.
Board revisions. V2 adds speaker, microphone and touch logo; the simulator shows a V2.

concepts: Flash = copy main.py to the (simulated) board and restart it.
print() output appears on serial; Ctrl+C in serial stops the program and opens the REPL, Ctrl+D restarts.
Code marked V2 (speaker, microphone, touch logo, audio.SoundEffect) runs in the simulator but not on a V1 board.
Keep logic in functions and guard the endless loop, so tests can call one iteration.

code:
# Lab 01 - first program: show an image and print to serial.
# Runs unchanged in the micro:bit Python Editor simulator and on a V1/V2 board.
from microbit import *   # stub tests swap in labs/sim_stub: same API, fake hardware


def hello():
    # Runs once at start-up.
    display.show(Image.HAPPY)
    print("hello from micro:bit")   # serial: print() text goes to the serial panel


def step(count):
    # One loop iteration: print a counter so you can watch the serial panel.
    count += 1
    print("tick", count)
    return count


def main():
    hello()
    count = 0
    while True:
        count = step(count)
        sleep(1000)  # milliseconds; in the stub only a virtual clock advances


# main.py runs as __main__ on the board/simulator (flash = copy + restart);
# unit tests import it under another name, so the endless loop does not start.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Lab 02 - the 5x5 LED display: scroll text, built-in and custom images,
# per-pixel brightness (0 = off .. 9 = brightest).
from microbit import *

# Custom image: one string per row, digits are brightness, ":" ends a row.
# display buffer: these 25 numbers are what the driver scans onto the LEDs.
DIAMOND = Image("00900:"
                "09590:"
                "95159:"
                "09590:"
                "00900")


def intro():
    display.scroll("Hi")          # blocking call: returns only after the text has scrolled past
    display.show(Image.HEART)     # built-in image (read-only: copy() before editing)
    sleep(500)
    display.show(DIAMOND)         # show() replaces the whole buffer
    sleep(500)
    print("intro done")


def level_image(level):
    # Whole display at one brightness level.
    img = Image()                 # blank 5x5
    img.fill(level)               # per-pixel brightness 0-9 (not 0-255 as in MakeCode)
    return img


def step(level):
    # One loop iteration: show the next brightness level and log it.
    display.show(level_image(level))
    print("brightness", level)
    return (level + 1) % 10       # 0..9 then wrap


def main():
    intro()
    level = 0
    while True:
        level = step(level)
        sleep(200)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

title: Buttons
description: Use is_pressed, was_pressed and get_presses on buttons A and B to build a counter.
outcome: You can pick the right button call: held now, pressed since last check, or number of presses.
environment: micro:bit Python Editor v3 (python.microbit.org) with its MicroPython micro:bit V2 simulator (iframe python-simulator.usermbit.org/v/0.1; MIT; embeds MicroPython for micro:bit 2.1.1 per the repo's lib folder). Local: Python 3.12 stdlib + labs/sim_stub. CI: Node 24 + @playwright/test 1.64.1. Hosts: Apple-silicon Mac mini (macOS 14+) and Windows 11, same browser simulator; tests run with python3 (macOS) / py (Windows); see documentation/HARDWARE.md.
overview: is_pressed() reports the button right now; was_pressed() and get_presses() remember presses between checks and reset when read.

glossary.meaning: Checking an input repeatedly in a loop.
The moment a button goes from up to down (a 'press').

concepts: is_pressed(): level - True only while held.
was_pressed(): True once per press since the last call, then cleared.
get_presses(): running total since the last call, then reset to 0 - catches several quick presses.

code:
# Lab 03 - buttons: is_pressed (held now?) vs was_pressed (pressed since
# last check?) vs get_presses (how many presses since last check?).
from microbit import *


def step(count):
    # counted edges: get_presses() returns every press of A since the last
    # call (even several during one sleep), then resets to 0.
    count_before = count
    count += button_a.get_presses()
    # edge flag: was_pressed() is a single yes/no since last time, cleared on read.
    if button_b.was_pressed():
        count = 0
    if count != count_before:
        print("count", count)
        display.show(count % 10, wait=False)   # last digit, non-blocking
    # level: is_pressed() is true only while the button is held down right now.
    if button_a.is_pressed() and button_b.is_pressed():
        print("both held")
    return count


def main():
    print("A = +1, B = reset")
    count = 0
    while True:
        count = step(count)
        sleep(100)    # polling interval: presses between polls wait in the runtime


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

title: Sound
description: Play a melody and a pitch with music, a V2 built-in Sound and a custom SoundEffect, and switch the V2 speaker off/on.
outcome: You can make the micro:bit play notes, tones and sound effects and control where sound goes.
environment: micro:bit Python Editor v3 (python.microbit.org) with its MicroPython micro:bit V2 simulator (iframe python-simulator.usermbit.org/v/0.1; MIT; embeds MicroPython for micro:bit 2.1.1 per the repo's lib folder). Local: Python 3.12 stdlib + labs/sim_stub. CI: Node 24 + @playwright/test 1.64.1. Hosts: Apple-silicon Mac mini (macOS 14+) and Windows 11, same browser simulator; tests run with python3 (macOS) / py (Windows); see documentation/HARDWARE.md.

# Lab 04 - sound: music melodies and pitch, V2 built-in sounds, a custom
# SoundEffect, and switching the V2 speaker on/off.
# A = melody, B = speaker on/off, touch logo (V2) = sound effect.
from microbit import *
import music

# Note format: NOTE[octave][:ticks]; octave/ticks carry over to later notes.
# pitch + duration: c4 = 261.63 Hz; 1 tick = 125 ms at the default tempo.
TUNE = ["c4:2", "e", "g", "c5:4", "r:2", "g4:2", "c5:6"]

# V2 only. Rising triangle-wave sweep, 0.4 s.
# frequency over time: one slide from freq_start to freq_end.
SWEEP = audio.SoundEffect(freq_start=400, freq_end=2000, duration=400,
                          waveform=audio.SoundEffect.WAVEFORM_TRIANGLE)


def start():
    audio.play(Sound.HELLO)       # V2 built-in sound
    music.pitch(440, 200)         # concert A (A4 = 440 Hz) for 200 ms
    print("sound ready")


def step():
    if button_a.was_pressed():
        music.play(TUNE)          # blocking playback: the loop waits 2.5 s for the tune
        print("tune played")
    if button_b.was_pressed():
        if speaker.is_on():
            speaker.off()         # output taps: speaker closed, pin 0 output still works
        else:
            speaker.on()
        print("speaker", "on" if speaker.is_on() else "off")
    if pin_logo.is_touched():
        audio.play(SWEEP)
        print("effect played")


def main():
    start()
    while True:
        step()
        sleep(50)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Lab 05 - temperature and light: read both sensors, log to serial,
# and show a simple threshold result on the display.
from microbit import *

# named thresholds: tune them here, not deep inside the loop.
HOT_C = 26        # degrees Celsius (processor temperature, approximate)
DARK_LEVEL = 40   # light level 0..255, larger = brighter


def classify(temp_c, light):
    # classify: pure logic, easy to unit-test without any sensor.
    # Priority: dark is checked first, so it wins over hot.
    if light < DARK_LEVEL:
        return "dark"
    if temp_c >= HOT_C:   # single threshold (inclusive); hysteresis is the L200 upgrade
        return "hot"
    return "ok"


def step():
    # sample: whole degrees C from the processor; light by running LEDs in reverse.
    t = temperature()
    light = display.read_light_level()
    state = classify(t, light)
    # act: log key=value lines, then show the decision.
    print("temp={},light={},state={}".format(t, light, state))
    if state == "dark":
        display.show(Image.ASLEEP)
    elif state == "hot":
        display.show("H")
    else:
        display.show(Image.HAPPY)
    return state


def main():
    while True:
        step()
        sleep(1000)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
